newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bury "God's forgotten one" who died at 122.
newsitem.headline: French bury "God's forgotten one" who died at 122.

text.p: Jeanne Calment, the world's oldest person until her death this week at 122, was laid to rest in her hometown Arles in France's southern Provence region on Wednesday.
Calment, a living link back to a time without cars, telephones, movies or aircraft, died on Monday at the Maison du Lac retirement home where she had spent her last 12 years.
After a funeral service in a hospital chapel adjacent to the Maison du Lac, the cortege wound its way through the city towards the Trinquetaille cemetery.

The hearse carrying her body stopped for an instant outside the house where she spent some 100 years of her life and ran a clothing shop with her husband, who died in 1942, four years before their golden wedding anniversary.
Some 30 people, including employees of the nursing home and Arles Mayor Michel Vauzelle, were allowed into the cemetery with the coffin, draped in a French flag and a Provencal sash.
Disappointed town residents who had fondly nicknamed her "Queen Jeanne" were kept outside. Local civilian and religious authorities are to stage a public tribute to her on Thursday.
The burial ceremony lasted a few minutes and Calment was laid to rest in a family tomb alongside her husband, her daughter, who died in 1934, and her grandson, a doctor who died in 1963.
Calment was listed by the Guinness Book of Records as the oldest, documented person alive when she reached the age of 120 years and 238 days.
She is now succeeded by Danish-American Christian Mortensen, who celebrated his 115th birthday as Calment was being buried.
Born on February 21, 1875, 10 years after the assassination of U.S. President Abraham Lincoln, Calment had passed 60, the retirement age, when Hitler's Nazis invaded France in 1940.
As a young girl in Arles, Calment met 19th century Impressionist master Vincent Van Gogh and described him as "ugly as a louse" and "boorish and impolite".
She remained lucid and kept a cheerful sense of humour to the end. "God must have forgotten me," she once said.
Scientists who studied records of Calment's ancestors have said most of them lived longer than average.
A scientific committee asked for a tiny sample of her brain to study the neurons as a possible key to her longevity, but Arles Hospital refused.
